extracted.intended_audience: students/scholars of humor theory, critics, writers and comedians interested in comic construction
extracted.subtask_description: Use Henri Bergson's framework for analyzing or creating comic effects, based on the central image of 'the mechanical encrusted on the living' and three formal laws (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference). Useful for diagnosing why something is funny or not and for structuring jokes, scenes, or characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical encrusted on the living (du mécanique plaqué sur du vivant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Central image: comedy arises when something mechanical is 'plated' onto the living — rigidity, automatism, or mechanical repetition appears where life expects elasticity and responsiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life is 'elastic, attentive, supple, and self-adjusting.' When a person shows the opposite (rigidity, automatism, distraction, mechanical repetition where flexibility was needed) they become comic. Laughter functions as a social corrective: it punishes or highlights failure to be 'attentively alive.' Use this contrast to locate or generate comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insensibility (anesthésie momentanée du cœur)
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience must temporarily suspend sympathy; comedy requires the heart to be still.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If pity or affection is aroused instead, laughter is destroyed. Comic situations typically distance the audience affectively so they can treat the subject as mechanical rather than suffering. When crafting or assessing a comic moment, check whether sympathy interferes with laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/social setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is essentially a group phenomenon; it relies on a social/public context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy functions as social correction — we laugh to realign or rejoin others. Material that only works in isolation (no public reference point) may fail to produce the communal aspect of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: A human reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Even nonhuman comedy (landscapes, animals, objects) is comic because it evokes something human; a human reference is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the comic element points back to a human quality or condition (a human shape, mannerism, intention). Purely abstract or non-human spectacle detached from human reference risks being non-comic according to Bergson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 1: Repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: A character, situation, or phrase repeats when life would have varied; the repeated element becomes increasingly mechanical-seeming each time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms of repetition include verbal (a catchphrase in absurd contexts), situational (the same scene replayed with different characters), and gesture (a tic appearing incongruously). Use escalating repetition to make the repeated element seem like a 'thing' rather than living action; the comic tension comes from life being expected to be unrepeatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 2: Inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation flips into its mirror image; roles reverse (e.g., the thief robbed, the judge in the dock).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal exposes the rigidity of the original arrangement by showing it working in reverse. Use role reversals or mirrored situations to reveal and ridicule institutional or personal stiffness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 3: Reciprocal Interference of Series
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation belongs simultaneously to two independent series of events, each consistent in itself, allowing two entirely different interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: misunderstandings where parties interpret events under different 'series,' vaudeville door-mistake collisions, and puns where a single utterance fits two chains of meaning. Craft scenes or lines that legitimately slot into two contexts so the clash produces comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects of ridicule that are formal — a face, a costume, a posture that has become rigid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for physiognomy, dress, or static postures that suggest mechanical fixation. These are well-suited to visual comedy and caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Awkward, mechanical, or repetitive bodily action that contrasts with expected supple movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical comedy, slapstick, and mannerism-driven jokes rely on movement appearing mechanical where adaptability is expected. Timing and exaggeration amplify the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot-level comedy produced by applying the three laws to situations (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structural devices (repeated scenes, role reversals, intersecting plot series) to build situational humor. Vaudeville and farce are typical forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Language-based comedy where the three laws operate on speech (repetition of phrases, verbal inversions, puns/multiple series of meaning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordplay, malapropisms, repeated catchphrases, and double-entendres exploit linguistic structures to create mechanical-sounding language in contexts that call for subtlety or change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Personality-based comedy where traits (vanity, miserliness, distraction) become rigid and stereotyped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct characters whose dominant trait manifests as mechanical behavior across contexts; the comic arises when the trait fails to adapt to new demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: anything that arouses pity or affection
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson excludes any comic material that provokes pity or genuine affection — sympathy destroys laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating comedy, test whether the audience feels compassion; if so, the piece no longer functions as comic by Bergson's standard. Beware of mixing pathos with the intended ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: the genuinely flexible, attentive person
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who are truly attentive, elastic, and adaptive are not comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid depicting characters as simply eccentric; to be comic they must be rigid in a context that demands adaptability. Celebratory depictions of suppleness will not produce laughter under this framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: pure spectacle disconnected from human reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure spectacle that lacks human reference is excluded from comedic status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure visual or spectacular elements point back to human behavior or conditions; otherwise the spectatorship may be aesthetic but not comic per Bergson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist (questions to test for the comic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of practical questions to determine whether an event is comic under Bergson's criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions include: Is there rigidity, automatism, or absent-mindedness where adaptive response was expected? Does one of the three laws structure the comic event (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference)? Is sympathy temporarily suspended? Does the laughter function as social correction—making the rigid person realize they were being mechanical? Use these as a quick evaluative rubric when analyzing or creating comic moments.
